eligibility.evidence: Sec. I-III: GPT-4 (temperature 0, OpenAI API) is the subject. Study 1 re-administers the appraisal/emotion rating task of Skerry and Saxe (2015) with the same scales and wordings; Study 2 gives crowd-enVENT vignettes (Troiano et al. 2023). Cites the human studies (E2 test met); emotion attribution is social cognition. Borderline because Study 2 is a corpus-annotation (affective computing) task, not a lab paradigm.

A.title: GPT-4 Emulates Average-Human Emotional Cognition from a Third-Person Perspective
A.venue: International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII)

paradigms.name: Appraisal (38 variables, reduced to 10) and emotion-dimension (8) ratings of crafted emotion-evoking stimuli, Study 1; emotion classification derived from the ratings
Appraisal ratings (21 variables) and 13-way emotion labelling of self-reported vignettes, Study 2 (crowd-enVENT)
paradigms.source_paper: Troiano et al. 2023 (Computational Linguistics, crowd-enVENT corpus)

D.population: Study 1: MTurk raters from Skerry and Saxe (1521 responses; participant count not stated). Study 2: crowd-enVENT authors and five readers per vignette (online annotation corpus)
D.metric: Pearson r of stimulus means; Krippendorff alpha; classification accuracy; Jensen-Shannon divergence

effects.es_metric: Pearson r with human stimulus-mean ratings (range 0.528-0.945 across 10 appraisals; 0.671-0.970 across 8 emotion dimensions)
effects.label: AGREEMENT-ONLY
effects.location: Study 1, Table I and Table II (p<.001 stars); no single summary value reported

effects.es_metric: Krippendorff alpha (GPT-4 vs author self-report and vs average reader)
effects.label: AGREEMENT-ONLY
effects.location: Study 2, Fig. 8 and Fig. 9 (values only in figures, not in text); no test of the author-vs-reader difference

E.headline: GPT-4 closely matches average human appraisal and emotion ratings and aligns better with average third-person readers than with authors' self-assessments.

G.notes: Single unversioned GPT-4, no query date, no code or prompt release. Each Study 1 prompt repeated 8 times but with a random name each time. Fig. 8-9 values not in text. 'Significantly better' claims for reader vs author agreement have no test. Tested-by-correlation p-values only.
